passages.text: by HealthPartners

A steady rhythm to energize long workouts. Audiobooks to make chores more fun. A way to concentrate on work without being distracted by the background conversations of coworkers. These are just some of the reasons why people love earbuds and use them for hours at a time.
Still, many people have questions about earbud safety and if it’s okay to wear them so much. Are wireless earbuds safe? Is noise cancelling bad for your ears? Why do my earbuds hurt my ears?
Read on to learn about popular types of earbuds and how to use earbuds without damaging your ears.
Simply put, earbuds are small headphones that you wear inside your ear. Some, but not all, earbuds include a built-in microphone.
passages.heading_path: But first, what are earbuds?

passages.text: Earbuds are used for audio entertainment and communication. You can use them to listen to music, podcasts and movies. Earbuds with a mic are also helpful for hands-free communication – for example, as gaming earbuds or to take calls from your mobile phone or computer.
passages.heading_path: But first, what are earbuds?

passages.text: Since others cannot hear what you’re listening to when you wear earbuds, you can wear them around others without being disruptive. Earbuds can also cancel out background sounds, so you can hear audio content without being distracted by the people and noises around you.
passages.heading_path: But first, what are earbuds?

passages.text: Wearing earbuds is common during activities such as working, video calls, running, online gaming and swimming.
passages.heading_path: But first, what are earbuds?

passages.text: The sound you hear through your headphones is not the same as the sound produced by your device. One of the main functions of earbuds is to change electrical energy from your listening device into sound waves and to transmit the signals to your ear so you can hear them – usually as vibrations that travel through your ear canal to your eardrum.
passages.heading_path: But first, what are earbuds? > How earbuds work

passages.text: There are many types of earbuds, and it seems that there are more options every day. The biggest differences tend to be how the earbuds fit and the technology behind them – and these differences can affect headphone safety (we’ll get to that later in the post).
passages.heading_path: Differences in the types of earbuds

passages.text: Wired earbuds plug in directly to your phone, computer, tablet or other device. When you turn on a song or a story, the sound travels through the headphones wire as electrical current. When the electrical current reaches the headphones, it’s turned into sound waves which are responsible for the sounds we hear.
passages.heading_path: Differences in the types of earbuds > Wired earbuds

passages.text: Wireless earbuds do not have a cable leading to your phone or device. But some styles of wireless earbuds have a flexible strap that connects the right earbud to the left earbud. Most wireless earbuds are Bluetooth earbuds, meaning they use short-range microwaves to wirelessly send electrical signals from your device to the headphones.
passages.heading_path: Differences in the types of earbuds > Wired earbuds

passages.text: All earbuds that fit in your ear canal block out some noise since they create a physical barrier between your eardrum and the outside world. But noise-cancelling earbuds do more to block out the noise – they change how your ears hear through inverse audio. Active noise-cancelling earbuds use tiny microphones and complicated circuitry that produce outgoing soundwaves that are opposite of the soundwaves coming in from your environment.
passages.heading_path: Differences in the types of earbuds > Noise-cancelling earbuds

passages.text: But active cancellation doesn’t work for everyone – some people can still hear background noise. It’s also possible that you may find active noise cancellation uncomfortable or have side effects such as headaches, dizziness and nausea.
passages.heading_path: Differences in the types of earbuds > Noise-cancelling earbuds

passages.text: Bone conduction earbuds fit differently than other earbuds. Instead of going into your ears, they usually sit on your temples. They also work differently, sending vibrations through the bones of your head and jaw to your inner ear. Some people might find the sensation uncomfortable and have headaches, vertigo or dizziness when using them.
passages.heading_path: Differences in the types of earbuds > Bone conduction earbuds

passages.text: Since the sound doesn’t go through the eardrum, these types of earbuds can work for people with hearing problems. In fact, bone conduction technology has been used in hearing aids for hundreds of years.
passages.heading_path: Differences in the types of earbuds > Bone conduction earbuds

passages.text: The downside is that these types of headphones don’t block as much background noise as in-ear headphones. But the plus side is that you’re more aware of your surroundings – something that’s definitely valuable if you’re using earbuds while doing outside activities like running.
passages.heading_path: Differences in the types of earbuds > Bone conduction earbuds

passages.text: While earbuds make life more interesting and enjoyable, there are some earbuds health risks you should know about.
passages.heading_path: The big question: Are earbuds bad for your ears?

passages.text: The biggest potential risk of using earbuds is hearing loss and tinnitus resulting from damage to your inner ear.
passages.heading_path: The big question: Are earbuds bad for your ears? > Hearing loss from earbuds

passages.text: In-ear earbuds play music directly into your ear canal. When the soundwave from the music reaches your eardrum, it creates a vibration that’s passed through the tiny bones of your middle ear and then into your inner ear.
passages.heading_path: The big question: Are earbuds bad for your ears? > Hearing loss from earbuds

passages.text: Your inner ear is covered with delicate hair cells and the vibrations cause these hairs to move. This movement creates an electrical impulse that’s sent to the brain where it’s interpreted as sound. If your music is too loud, it can permanently damage these hair cells, making it so they don’t send out electrical impulses in response to vibration. And, without these electrical impulses, your brain doesn’t know there’s anything to hear, or what it does hear may sound unclear or distorted.
passages.heading_path: The big question: Are earbuds bad for your ears? > Hearing loss from earbuds

passages.text: Here’s a fact that comes as no surprise: earbuds can get very dirty. For starters, there’s earwax, oil from your skin and dried sweat from your ears. Then there’s dirt and grime that collect when the earbuds aren’t being used.
passages.heading_path: The big question: Are earbuds bad for your ears? > Irritation or ear infections from earbuds

passages.text: In most cases, dirty earbuds are just gross, but they can also increase your risk of infection. Earbuds can get covered in bacteria, fungus or skin irritants that could get into your ear canal when you insert them – but that doesn’t necessarily mean you’ll get an ear infection .
passages.heading_path: The big question: Are earbuds bad for your ears? > Irritation or ear infections from earbuds

passages.text: Usually, your earwax helps protect you from dirt, fungi and bacteria when it gets in your ears. Still, there are a few reasons why earbud users are more likely to get ear infections:
passages.heading_path: The big question: Are earbuds bad for your ears? > Irritation or ear infections from earbuds

passages.text: Damage to the ear canal or eardrum – When there’s damage to your ear, the bacteria or fungi can find a way into your body, causing an infection. If the skin in your ear canal is scratched or irritated, you’re more likely to get an outer ear infection also known as swimmer’s ear . If you have a burst eardrum from listening to music too loudly, it increases your chance of a middle ear infection.
passages.heading_path: The big question: Are earbuds bad for your ears? > Irritation or ear infections from earbuds

passages.text: Warmth and moisture – Bacteria and fungi grow in warm, wet places. When you wear earbuds, that’s exactly the environment you create inside your ears.
passages.heading_path: The big question: Are earbuds bad for your ears? > Irritation or ear infections from earbuds

passages.text: Impacted earwax – Wearing earbuds can lead to earwax buildup. While earwax protects your ears, it’s possible to have too much. Impacted earwax can trap dirty water, fungi and bacteria, making it more likely that you’ll develop ear infections.
passages.heading_path: The big question: Are earbuds bad for your ears? > Irritation or ear infections from earbuds

passages.text: You may wonder, do earbuds emit radiation? The answer is yes. Bluetooth wireless earbuds send out non-ionizing electromagnetic radiation (EMR), mostly as microwaves. And wired earbuds emit extremely low frequency (ELF) radiation.
passages.heading_path: The big question: Are earbuds bad for your ears? > Radiation exposure from wireless earbuds

passages.text: At this point, there is no conclusive evidence that earbud radiation is harmful. Earbuds are pretty new, and we don’t know if there will be long-term effects from earbud radiation. Still, earbuds are generally considered safe by the scientific community.
passages.heading_path: The big question: Are earbuds bad for your ears? > Radiation exposure from wireless earbuds

passages.text: Given the earbud health risks, maybe you’re wondering if there are better options to listen to your tunes and podcasts at work or at the mall.
passages.heading_path: Are there safer options for listening on the go?

passages.text: Yes, headphones are somewhat safer than earbuds for a couple of reasons. They don’t go in the ear, so there’s less risk of infections. Plus, your audio content isn’t pumped directly into your ear canal – but you can still get hearing damage with headphones if you listen too loudly.
passages.heading_path: Are there safer options for listening on the go? > Are headphones safer than earbuds?

citations.sentence_text: The evidence indicates that over-ear headphones are generally safer than earbuds for long-term ear health, particularly regarding infection risk and earwax impaction.
citations.audit_note: Passage supports that headphones are safer due to reduced infection risk, but does not mention earwax impaction.

citations.sentence_text: Headphones do not go into the ear canal, reducing the risk of ear infections and wax impaction.
citations.audit_note: Passage supports reduced infection risk but not wax impaction.

citations.sentence_text: However, both headphones and earbuds can cause hearing damage if used at high volumes.
citations.audit_note: Passage supports that headphones can cause hearing damage at high volumes but does not mention earbuds.

citations.sentence_text: HealthPartners states that headphones are somewhat safer than earbuds due to less infection risk and less direct sound into the ear canal.
citations.audit_note: Passage supports the claim that headphones are safer due to less infection risk and less direct sound, but does not attribute it to HealthPartners.

passages.text: It’s possible. For one thing, bone conduction earbuds don’t go in the ear canal, so there’s less risk of ear infections. They also won’t cause hearing loss from a ruptured eardrum. But if you misuse bone conduction earbuds, it’s still possible to damage your inner ear, causing hearing loss.
passages.heading_path: Are there safer options for listening on the go? > Are bone conduction earbuds safer than traditional earbuds?

passages.text: Bone conductions are also newer technology, meaning we don’t yet know the long-term effects of using these types of headphones.
passages.heading_path: Are there safer options for listening on the go? > Are bone conduction earbuds safer than traditional earbuds?

passages.text: You don’t need to ditch your favorite pair of earbuds or switch to headphones or a bone conduction option. By taking steps to use your earbuds correctly, you can reduce the chance of hurting your ears or hearing.
passages.heading_path: How to use earbuds safely

passages.text: Your best resource will be the instruction booklet that comes with your earbuds. But here are a few things to keep in mind:
passages.heading_path: How to use earbuds safely > How to wear wired and wireless earbuds

passages.text: Ensure the right fit – If your earbuds come with different tips, make sure you’re choosing the ones that are sized for your ears. If they’re too large, they could hurt your ear canal.
passages.heading_path: How to use earbuds safely > How to wear wired and wireless earbuds

passages.text: Put them in the correct ears – You’ll notice each earbud has an R or L corresponding to the right and left ears. You may hurt your ear canal if you put the earbuds in the wrong ears. Plus, sound quality will likely suffer.
passages.heading_path: How to use earbuds safely > How to wear wired and wireless earbuds

passages.text: Insert at the correct angle – When inserting earbuds, angle them up and toward the front of your head. This will help create a better fit since the ear canal angles toward the front and top of your head.
passages.heading_path: How to use earbuds safely > How to wear wired and wireless earbuds

passages.text: Make sure your ears are clean – If your ears are dirty, you may be more likely to get an infection. Plus, you won’t be able to hear audio content as clearly. But to make sure you don’t hurt your ear canal, clean your ears without Q-tips .
passages.heading_path: How to use earbuds safely > How to wear wired and wireless earbuds

passages.text: Hearing loss due to earbuds is 100% preventable – you just need to make sure the volume isn’t too loud.
passages.heading_path: How to use earbuds safely > How to keep earbuds at a safe volume

passages.text: Have you ever wondered, how loud is too loud? To answer that question, we’ll talk briefly about decibels (dB), a measurement used to determine how loud sounds are and if they are safe or could affect your hearing.
passages.heading_path: How to use earbuds safely > How to keep earbuds at a safe volume

passages.text: Decibels measure the pressure levels created by different volumes of sound. When your ears are exposed to high decibel levels, the resulting pressure can damage your ears. The decibel range goes from 0 dB (sounds so quiet we can’t hear them) to 140 dB (sounds so loud that they cause pain). Listening to anything over 85 dB for a large amount of time can cause permanent hearing loss. To put that in context, a nearby alarm clock is about 80 dB and a blender is 90 dB.
passages.heading_path: How to use earbuds safely > How to keep earbuds at a safe volume

passages.text: If you’re an adult, try to keep your earbud volume between 60 dB and 85 dB. Kids’ ears are more sensitive and more likely to get damaged. To avoid hearing loss in children, make sure they’re using kids’ headphones that limit the maximum volume to less than 82 dB.
passages.heading_path: How to use earbuds safely > How to keep earbuds at a safe volume > Decibel levels of common sounds

passages.text: Because here’s the thing: The volume on most listening devices can be cranked up beyond what’s safe for human ears. For example, Apple devices can go over 100 dB. So watch the volume bar and try not to go above 70% of total volume. Also, watch for warnings from your phone or device. If it tells you that your audio volume is too loud, turn down the sound.
passages.heading_path: How to use earbuds safely > How to keep earbuds at a safe volume > Decibel levels of common sounds

passages.text: Your best bet is to listen at as low a volume as possible. If you’re always cranking up the volume to block out background noise, you may want to give noise-cancelling headphones a try.
passages.heading_path: How to use earbuds safely > How to keep earbuds at a safe volume > Decibel levels of common sounds

passages.text: It’s best to give your ears a break every couple of hours – even five minutes without tunes can help. This will give your ears a rest from the intense vibrations that come with listening with earbuds.
passages.heading_path: How to use earbuds safely > Take regular breaks

passages.text: Since bacteria and fungi like to grow in dark, moist places, pulling out the earbuds also gives your ear canal a chance to air out, reducing your chance of infections.
passages.heading_path: How to use earbuds safely > Take regular breaks

passages.text: Plus, removing your earbuds gives you a chance to hear what’s going on in the world and to interact with others.
passages.heading_path: How to use earbuds safely > Take regular breaks

passages.text: Clean earbuds are safer, last longer and sound better. But how often should you clean your earbuds? The answer depends on how you use them. If you use your earbuds while doing indoor household chores and you keep them on your desk, you can probably just clean them once every week or two. But if you use them a lot or during sports, you’ll likely need to clean them more often.
passages.heading_path: How to use earbuds safely > How to clean earbuds (and when to do it)

passages.text: If you regularly use your earbuds, try to give them a quick clean every couple of weeks. Here are the steps:
passages.heading_path: How to use earbuds safely > How to clean earbuds (and when to do it) > A quick clean every week or two

passages.text: Disconnect from power – Wired earbuds should be unplugged from your device. Wireless earbuds should be powered off.
passages.heading_path: How to use earbuds safely > How to clean earbuds (and when to do it) > A quick clean every week or two

passages.text: Use a damp cloth to wipe off the earbud tips – You can use plain water, soapy water or rubbing alcohol to wipe them down. The cloth should not be drippy – if fluid gets into the headphone circuitry, it could affect how well they work. For the same reason, you should not submerge your earbuds unless they are waterproof.
passages.heading_path: How to use earbuds safely > How to clean earbuds (and when to do it) > A quick clean every week or two

passages.text: Dry before storage – Use a microfiber cloth to dry your earbuds immediately after cleaning.
passages.heading_path: How to use earbuds safely > How to clean earbuds (and when to do it) > A quick clean every week or two

passages.text: If your earbuds get covered in sweat or water, rinse and dry them as soon as you can. Your earbuds should be completely dry before charging or storage. If you’re at the gym or pool and don’t have time to allow them to dry before storing them, put them in a plastic bag with a silicone gel pack until you get home.
passages.heading_path: How to use earbuds safely > How to clean earbuds (and when to do it) > Dry off after sweaty or wet activities

passages.text: The best way to know if your earbuds need a bigger clean is to look at them. If they are covered in earwax, dust, oil, sweat or sticky fingerprints, they need to be cleaned. Here are the steps:
passages.heading_path: How to use earbuds safely > How to clean earbuds (and when to do it) > A bigger clean when needed

passages.text: Pull off the ear tips and then gently remove the wax. An inexpensive earwax removal tool can make the process much easier. The loop side of the tool can help you scoop out the earwax, and the brush end helps to loosen any residue left on the earbuds. You can also use an unused toothbrush for this step.
passages.heading_path: How to use earbuds safely > How to clean earbuds (and when to do it) > A bigger clean when needed

passages.text: Wipe the earbuds using a cloth dampened with soapy water – dish detergent usually works best.
passages.heading_path: How to use earbuds safely > How to clean earbuds (and when to do it) > A bigger clean when needed

passages.text: Dry with a microfiber cloth.
passages.heading_path: How to use earbuds safely > How to clean earbuds (and when to do it) > A bigger clean when needed

passages.text: If you have AirPods or other earbuds that are stored in a case, you’ll want to take time to clean the connectors and the case. A dry cloth can work. Another option is a moistened (but not dripping) Q-tip. If there’s any residue on the connectors, use the cleaning tool to gently remove it.
passages.heading_path: How to use earbuds safely > How to clean earbuds (and when to do it) > A bigger clean when needed

passages.text: Always make sure your earbuds are clean and completely dry before storing them in a case. If you don’t have a case, try to store your earbuds in a place where they won’t get dirty. If you’re worried about humidity, it can be helpful to store them in a bag with a silica gel pack.
passages.heading_path: How to use earbuds safely > How to store earbuds

passages.text: Earbuds are usually safe when used correctly. Still, it’s possible to damage your ears or hearing. Make an appointment with your primary care doctor or clinician if you notice hearing loss or signs of an ear infection such as redness, itchiness, ear pain, ear discharge, hearing changes or fever.
passages.heading_path: Worried about your ears? We hear you.

passages.text: Primary care doctors can diagnose and treat hundreds of conditions. They’ll talk with you about your symptoms, and work with you to create a treatment plan. And if you need more advanced care, they can refer you to an audiologist who specializes in diagnostic hearing tests, or an ear, nose and throat (ENT) doctor who can treat underlying conditions that may be contributing to hearing issues.
passages.heading_path: Worried about your ears? We hear you.

passages.heading_path: Do Earbuds Cause Hearing Loss? > Key takeaways:

passages.text: Earbuds usually cause hearing loss when you listen to music that’s too loud. They can also cause hearing loss if you listen to music for too long, even if the volume is low.
passages.heading_path: Do Earbuds Cause Hearing Loss? > Key takeaways:

passages.text: Earbuds aren’t more dangerous than headphones. They both cause hearing loss in the same way.
passages.heading_path: Do Earbuds Cause Hearing Loss? > Key takeaways:

passages.text: These days, smartphones allow you to listen to music, podcasts, audiobooks, and more wherever you are. Advances in earbuds and headphones let you tune in almost anytime. As a result, lots of people are listening to their earbuds at high volumes for many hours per day. But is all of this noise safe?
passages.heading_path: Do Earbuds Cause Hearing Loss? > Key takeaways:

passages.text: While it’s possible to use earbuds safely, lots of people unknowingly put themselves at risk for hearing loss. This is because hearing loss can be caused by listening to things that are too loud or for too long — even when the volume isn’t very high.
passages.heading_path: Do Earbuds Cause Hearing Loss? > Key takeaways:

passages.text: So, exactly how loud is too loud? And when should you take your earbuds out to give your ears a rest? Keep reading to learn how earbuds can affect your hearing.
passages.heading_path: Do Earbuds Cause Hearing Loss? > Key takeaways:

passages.text: Whether earbuds are bad for your ears depends on how you use them. If earbuds are used the right way, they can be perfectly safe.
passages.heading_path: Do Earbuds Cause Hearing Loss? > Are earbuds bad for your ears?

passages.text: But unfortunately, it’s all too easy to use them incorrectly — and put your hearing at risk.
passages.heading_path: Do Earbuds Cause Hearing Loss? > Are earbuds bad for your ears?

passages.text: Imagine you’re walking down a loud street, listening to music through your earbuds. It’s natural to turn up the volume to hear your music over the bustling sounds of the street. Or you might leave your earbuds in to listen to music for hours on end while doing other activities. While these habits may not seem like a big deal, they can both put you at risk for hearing loss.
passages.heading_path: Do Earbuds Cause Hearing Loss? > Are earbuds bad for your ears?

passages.text: Your risk depends on two things: how loud you listen and how long you listen. For example, listening to music at 105 decibels (dB) can cause permanent hearing loss in as little as 15 minutes — 105 dB is roughly as loud as a subway car. On the other hand, if you listen at just 75 dB — about the volume of an average vacuum cleaner — you can safely listen to anything for over 16 hours .

passages.speaker: Your risk depends on two things

passages.text: Most people use earbuds at volumes between 75 dB and 105 dB, so how dangerous they are depends on how loud and how long you use them.

passages.text: Your inner ear contains thousands of tiny hairs called stereocilia . These hairs help your body convert sound waves into chemical reactions that your brain interprets as noise. When your ears are exposed to sounds that are too loud or for too long, these stereocilia can become damaged, potentially leading to hearing loss.
passages.heading_path: Do Earbuds Cause Hearing Loss? > Are earbuds bad for your ears? > How does noise damage your hearing?

passages.text: Earbuds can cause noise-induced hearing loss (NHL). Noise-induced hearing loss is exactly what it sounds like — it’s what happens when too much noise causes you to lose your ability to hear.
passages.heading_path: Do Earbuds Cause Hearing Loss? > Are earbuds bad for your ears? > What hearing problems can result from wearing earbuds?

passages.text: NHL is a type of sensorineural hearing loss , meaning your ears have a problem sensing and transmitting sounds (as opposed to conductive hearing loss , where a physical blockage interferes with hearing).
passages.heading_path: Do Earbuds Cause Hearing Loss? > Are earbuds bad for your ears? > What hearing problems can result from wearing earbuds?

passages.text: NHL can happen in two ways: suddenly or over time. Sudden hearing loss happens when you hear a short, loud noise. This can happen at volumes of about 140 dB, which is the volume of a nearby siren or gunshot. But most earbuds don’t get this loud, so it’s rare for them to cause sudden NHL.
passages.heading_path: Do Earbuds Cause Hearing Loss? > Are earbuds bad for your ears? > What hearing problems can result from wearing earbuds?
passages.speaker: NHL can happen in two ways

passages.text: Gradual NHL happens after years and years of listening to volumes that are just a bit too loud. Most people who get NHL from earbuds get it this way. Because gradual NHL happens so slowly, some people don’t notice the hearing loss until it’s too late.
passages.heading_path: Do Earbuds Cause Hearing Loss? > Are earbuds bad for your ears? > Read more like this > Explore these related articles, suggested for readers like you.

passages.text: And unfortunately, you can’t typically reverse hearing loss from headphones or earbuds.
passages.heading_path: Do Earbuds Cause Hearing Loss? > Are earbuds bad for your ears? > Read more like this > Explore these related articles, suggested for readers like you.

passages.text: If you’re worried about noise-induced hearing loss from your earbuds, watch out for the following symptoms :
passages.heading_path: Do Earbuds Cause Hearing Loss? > If you use earbuds, what hearing loss symptoms should you watch for?

passages.text: Sounds seem distorted or muffled
passages.heading_path: Do Earbuds Cause Hearing Loss? > If you use earbuds, what hearing loss symptoms should you watch for?

passages.text: Difficulty hearing high-pitched sounds
passages.heading_path: Do Earbuds Cause Hearing Loss? > If you use earbuds, what hearing loss symptoms should you watch for?

passages.text: Trouble understanding people, especially in loud or crowded places like restaurants or parties
passages.heading_path: Do Earbuds Cause Hearing Loss? > If you use earbuds, what hearing loss symptoms should you watch for?

passages.text: Difficulty hearing someone over the phone
passages.heading_path: Do Earbuds Cause Hearing Loss? > If you use earbuds, what hearing loss symptoms should you watch for?

passages.text: Difficulty telling the difference between certain sounds (like not telling the difference between the letters “s” and “f”)
passages.heading_path: Do Earbuds Cause Hearing Loss? > If you use earbuds, what hearing loss symptoms should you watch for?

passages.text: Needing to turn up the volume very high on the TV or radio
passages.heading_path: Do Earbuds Cause Hearing Loss? > If you use earbuds, what hearing loss symptoms should you watch for?

passages.text: Frequently asking others to speak up, to speak more clearly, or repeat themselves
passages.heading_path: Do Earbuds Cause Hearing Loss? > If you use earbuds, what hearing loss symptoms should you watch for?

passages.text: Certain sounds irritate you or are even painful
passages.heading_path: Do Earbuds Cause Hearing Loss? > If you use earbuds, what hearing loss symptoms should you watch for?

passages.text: A ringing in your ears, known as tinnitus
passages.heading_path: Do Earbuds Cause Hearing Loss? > If you use earbuds, what hearing loss symptoms should you watch for?

passages.text: If you experience any of these symptoms, you should see your primary care provider to schedule a hearing test.
passages.heading_path: Do Earbuds Cause Hearing Loss? > If you use earbuds, what hearing loss symptoms should you watch for?

passages.text: The best way to prevent hearing loss from earbuds is to turn the volume down. If your volume is low enough, you don’t have to worry about how long you use your earbuds. A good rule of thumb is to see if you can hear a normal conversation while wearing your earbuds. If you can, your volume is probably at a safe listening level.
passages.heading_path: Do Earbuds Cause Hearing Loss? > How can you prevent hearing loss from using earbuds?

passages.text: Most modern smartphones also include headphone safety features to help protect your hearing. By using these features, you can limit the volume coming from your earbuds. This is helpful because you’ll never have to wonder if your volume is too high ever again — your phone simply won’t allow your earbuds to get too loud.
passages.heading_path: Do Earbuds Cause Hearing Loss? > How can you prevent hearing loss from using earbuds?

passages.text: Here’s how to set up volume limits on your smartphone:
passages.heading_path: Do Earbuds Cause Hearing Loss? > How can you prevent hearing loss from using earbuds?

passages.text: For iPhone users: In settings, find the “Headphone Safety” feature and click “Reduce Loud Sounds.”
passages.heading_path: Do Earbuds Cause Hearing Loss? > How can you prevent hearing loss from using earbuds?
passages.speaker: For iPhone users

passages.text: For Android users: Go to the “Sounds and Vibration” settings and choose “Media Volume Limit.”
passages.heading_path: Do Earbuds Cause Hearing Loss? > How can you prevent hearing loss from using earbuds?
passages.speaker: For Android users

passages.text: The World Health Organization recommends setting the volume levels to 80 dB or below , or about 60% of the maximum possible volume. You can also access these features with parental controls to limit the volume on your child’s device.
passages.heading_path: Do Earbuds Cause Hearing Loss? > How can you prevent hearing loss from using earbuds?

passages.text: Possibly. People often listen to music at dangerously high volumes to drown out environmental noise. But noise-canceling earbuds automatically cancel out most environmental noise. This means you don’t need to turn the volume up as high, making it safer for your ears.
passages.heading_path: Do Earbuds Cause Hearing Loss? > How can you prevent hearing loss from using earbuds? > Can noise-canceling earbuds protect your ears?

passages.text: Because earbuds fit inside your ear canal, lots of people think they can cause more hearing loss than headphones.
passages.heading_path: Do Earbuds Cause Hearing Loss? > Which is better for your ears: Earbuds or headphones?

passages.text: But the truth is that it doesn’t matter whether you use earbuds or headphones. Neither is more dangerous than the other. The only things that matter when it comes to hearing loss are volume levels, and time. It doesn’t matter what’s making the noise.
passages.heading_path: Do Earbuds Cause Hearing Loss? > Which is better for your ears: Earbuds or headphones?

passages.text: That said, headphones can sometimes be safer than earbuds because they often block outside noise better. Many headphones cover your entire ear, which muffles noise from the outside world (even if they aren’t technically noise-canceling). This lets you listen at lower volumes, which can help protect your hearing.
passages.heading_path: Do Earbuds Cause Hearing Loss? > Which is better for your ears: Earbuds or headphones?

passages.text: The short answer is no. Like cell phones and televisions, wireless Bluetooth earbuds emit radiofrequency radiation . But radiofrequency radiation is both low frequency and low energy. This means it’s not powerful enough to damage DNA. (High-energy radiation, like X-rays and radon, can damage DNA.)
passages.heading_path: Do Earbuds Cause Hearing Loss? > Should you be worried about radiation exposure from wireless earbuds?

passages.text: While the human body does absorb radiofrequency radiation, the amount is not enough to negatively affect you in any way. According to the National Cancer Institute , there are no “dangerous health effects on the human body from radiofrequency radiation.” In other words, you can use earbuds without worrying about radiation.
passages.heading_path: Do Earbuds Cause Hearing Loss? > Should you be worried about radiation exposure from wireless earbuds?

passages.text: Earbuds can be dangerous for your hearing, but not necessarily for the reasons you might think. Earbuds aren’t dangerous because they sit inside your ear canal or emit radiation. They’re dangerous simply because they make noise. Listening to any noise that’s too loud or for too long can permanently damage your hearing, a condition known as noise-induced hearing loss.
passages.heading_path: Do Earbuds Cause Hearing Loss? > The bottom line

passages.text: To protect yourself, keep the volume low when using earbuds or headphones. Ideally, you should keep the volume under 80 dB, or no more than 60% of your device’s maximum volume. And if you’ve noticed any signs of hearing loss, be sure to check in with a healthcare professional to talk about next steps.

passages.text: With modern lifestyles revolving around music, podcasts, virtual meetings, and on-the-go communication, headphones and earbuds have become everyday essentials. This technology offers remarkable convenience and immersive sound experiences, allowing us to stay connected, entertained, and productive almost anywhere. However, an increasing number of people face health risks from chronic headphone use—especially when listening for extended hours at high volumes. Understanding how headphones can impact your ear health is the first step toward enjoying your favorite sounds responsibly and protecting your hearing for the long term.
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention

passages.text: If you’re like most people, headphones are a constant in your daily routine—whether during workouts, commutes, remote work calls, or unwinding at night. Recent years have seen a notable increase in headphone and earbud use, particularly among young adults and teens who rely on them for social interaction, entertainment, and education.
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > The Rise of Headphone Use and Why It Matters

passages.text: The term “chronic use” generally refers to wearing headphones or earbuds for prolonged periods—often several hours daily—frequently at moderate to high volumes. For instance, someone who listens to music or podcasts for several hours during their commute, plus additional use during workouts or relaxing, may unknowingly put their ear health at risk. It’s like consistently putting your ears under strain without letting them rest.
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > The Rise of Headphone Use and Why It Matters

passages.text: While headphones enrich our lives, constant use can quietly affect the delicate structures inside the ear. Unfortunately, many people remain unaware of the risks or the simple, proactive steps they can take to maintain healthy ears for years to come. Research shows that hearing loss related to headphone use is rising, especially among younger populations. This trend highlights the importance of education and adopting safe listening habits early on. Being mindful of your listening habits today makes a difference tomorrow.
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > The Rise of Headphone Use and Why It Matters

passages.text: Even if you don’t “crank” the volume, chronic headphone use introduces several potential risks. Let’s explore them in detail:
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > Understanding the Risks to Your Ear Health

passages.text: Noise-induced hearing loss is the most significant and lasting risk linked to headphone use. Loud sounds—typically those above 85 decibels (dB)—can damage the sensitive hair cells inside your inner ear. These tiny hair cells convert sound waves into electrical signals that your brain interprets as sound. When damaged or destroyed, hearing loss is permanent and irreversible.
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > Understanding the Risks to Your Ear Health > Noise-Induced Hearing Loss (NIHL)

passages.text: To put this in perspective, 80 dB is roughly equivalent to city traffic heard from inside a car. Listening to sounds above 85 dB for extended periods increases the risk of permanent hearing damage. At 80 dB, damage usually accumulates with longer exposure times, potentially developing after several hours, rather than minutes. For example, a loud concert or noisy construction site poses similar risks; with headphones, the impact may be greater because sound is delivered directly into the ear canal.
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > Understanding the Risks to Your Ear Health > Noise-Induced Hearing Loss (NIHL)

passages.text: Common symptoms of NIHL include:
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > Understanding the Risks to Your Ear Health > Noise-Induced Hearing Loss (NIHL)

passages.text: Ringing or buzzing in the ears (tinnitus)
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > Understanding the Risks to Your Ear Health > Noise-Induced Hearing Loss (NIHL)

passages.text: Difficulty understanding speech, especially in noisy environments
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > Understanding the Risks to Your Ear Health > Noise-Induced Hearing Loss (NIHL)

passages.text: Sounds appearing muffled or distorted
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > Understanding the Risks to Your Ear Health > Noise-Induced Hearing Loss (NIHL)

passages.text: Many audiologists recommend adopting the “60/60 Rule”: listening for no more than 60 minutes at 60% of your device’s maximum volume, then taking a break to let your ears recover. Research suggests keeping volume levels at or below 60% avoids excessive noise exposure, lowering the risk of damage. Additionally, total safe listening time at 80 dB is about 40 hours per week; exceeding these guidelines may increase the risk of hearing loss.
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > Understanding the Risks to Your Ear Health > Noise-Induced Hearing Loss (NIHL)

passages.text: According to audiologists like Dr. Emily Carter, “Many patients don’t realize that it’s not just how loud you listen, but also how long you listen that matters. Even moderate volumes can cause harm if used excessively.” Hearing damage often develops gradually, so early prevention is critical. Protecting your ears now preserves your hearing for years to come.
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > Understanding the Risks to Your Ear Health > Noise-Induced Hearing Loss (NIHL)

passages.text: Besides hearing loss, frequent earbud use can increase the risk of outer ear infections known as otitis externa. Earbuds and in-ear headphones can trap sweat, moisture, and bacteria inside the ear canal, creating a warm, damp environment that encourages microbial growth. This risk is particularly high during workouts, hot weather, or when earbuds are shared or not cleaned regularly.
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > Understanding the Risks to Your Ear Health > Ear Infections Linked to Headphone Use

passages.text: Signs of headphone-related ear infections may include:
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > Understanding the Risks to Your Ear Health > Ear Infections Linked to Headphone Use

passages.text: Itching or irritation inside the ear canal
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > Understanding the Risks to Your Ear Health > Ear Infections Linked to Headphone Use

passages.text: Redness, swelling, or pain around or inside the ear
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > Understanding the Risks to Your Ear Health > Ear Infections Linked to Headphone Use

passages.text: Unusual discharge or unpleasant odor
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > Understanding the Risks to Your Ear Health > Ear Infections Linked to Headphone Use

passages.text: It’s important to give your ears regular breaks and allow air to circulate. Using over-ear headphones, which generally allow better ventilation, may help reduce infection risk. Proper hygiene—such as wiping earbuds and washing hands before handling them—also makes a significant difference. For more detailed information, see What is an Ear Infection? . Keeping your ears clean and dry helps prevent infections.
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > Understanding the Risks to Your Ear Health > Ear Infections Linked to Headphone Use

passages.text: In addition to hearing loss and infections, chronic headphone use can cause other ear-related problems:
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > Understanding the Risks to Your Ear Health > Other Ear-Related Issues

passages.text: Excessive earwax buildup: Earbuds may potentially push earwax deeper into the canal in some users, causing blockages or discomfort. This buildup can sometimes lead to temporary muffled hearing or a feeling of fullness.
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > Understanding the Risks to Your Ear Health > Other Ear-Related Issues
passages.speaker: Excessive earwax buildup

passages.text: Ear canal irritation: Frequent insertion and removal of ill-fitting earbuds or headphones can irritate or cause small abrasions, making the skin sensitive or sore.
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > Understanding the Risks to Your Ear Health > Other Ear-Related Issues
passages.speaker: Ear canal irritation

passages.text: General discomfort or pressure: Extended use of tightly fitting headphones can exert pressure on the outer ear and surrounding skin, leading to soreness or irritation over time.
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > Understanding the Risks to Your Ear Health > Other Ear-Related Issues
passages.speaker: General discomfort or pressure

passages.text: All these issues emphasize the importance of monitoring your ear health and incorporating listening habits into your overall wellness routine. For more on ear irritation and swelling, visit Swollen Ear: What It Means . Awareness and care are keys to comfort and health.
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > Understanding the Risks to Your Ear Health > Other Ear-Related Issues

passages.text: The effects of chronic headphone use can be subtle at first, so watching for early warning signs is essential. Key symptoms include:
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > Recognizing Early Signs of Ear Damage

passages.text: Persistent ringing or buzzing in your ears (tinnitus), especially after headphone use
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > Recognizing Early Signs of Ear Damage

passages.text: Difficulty understanding speech in noisy settings or a general decline in hearing clarity
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > Recognizing Early Signs of Ear Damage

passages.text: Ear pain, itchiness, or discomfort following headphone use
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > Recognizing Early Signs of Ear Damage

passages.text: Feelings of fullness, pressure, or muffled hearing after wearing headphones
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > Recognizing Early Signs of Ear Damage

passages.text: If you notice any of these symptoms, it’s important to take action sooner rather than later. Early intervention can prevent further damage and improve outcomes. Many audiologists recommend prompt evaluation to detect early hearing loss or ear infections. Learn more about signs of hearing loss and when to see a doctor in What is Hearing Loss? Understanding Causes, Symptoms, and When To See a Doctor . Listening to your body can protect your hearing future.
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > Recognizing Early Signs of Ear Damage

passages.text: The good news is that most risks from chronic headphone use are avoidable through simple, conscientious habits. Incorporating safe listening routines can safeguard your hearing health for a lifetime.
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > How to Protect Your Ears from Headphone Damage

passages.text: Keep volume under 60%: Avoid turning the volume above 60% of the maximum. Many devices provide volume limit settings—consider enabling these to help manage levels.
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > How to Protect Your Ears from Headphone Damage > Manage Volume and Listening Time

passages.text: Practice the 60/60 Rule: Limit listening sessions to no more than 60 minutes at 60% volume before taking a break to rest your ears. This allows your inner ear cells time to recover.
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > How to Protect Your Ears from Headphone Damage > Manage Volume and Listening Time

passages.text: Monitor total exposure: Avoid exceeding approximately 40 hours per week at 80 dB or less when combining all headphone use.
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > How to Protect Your Ears from Headphone Damage > Manage Volume and Listening Time
passages.speaker: Monitor total exposure

passages.text: Use noise-canceling headphones: These devices actively block ambient noise, enabling you to listen comfortably at lower volumes, reducing ear strain. For example, commuters in noisy environments often find noise-canceling headphones help maintain lower volume settings without compromising sound clarity.
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > How to Protect Your Ears from Headphone Damage > Manage Volume and Listening Time
passages.speaker: Use noise-canceling headphones

passages.text: Avoid headphone use immediately before bedtime: This allows your ears adequate rest and can also improve sleep quality.
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > How to Protect Your Ears from Headphone Damage > Manage Volume and Listening Time
passages.speaker: Avoid headphone use immediately before bedtime

passages.text: Clean your headphones and earbuds regularly: Wipe them with a dry or lightly damp cloth frequently, especially after sweating or heavy use, to reduce bacterial buildup.
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > How to Protect Your Ears from Headphone Damage > Practice Proper Hygiene and Maintenance
passages.speaker: Clean your headphones and earbuds regularly

passages.text: Avoid sharing earbuds or headphones: Sharing may increase the risk of transferring germs and infections among users.
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > How to Protect Your Ears from Headphone Damage > Practice Proper Hygiene and Maintenance
passages.speaker: Avoid sharing earbuds or headphones

passages.text: Allow your ears to breathe: Take regular headphone breaks during the day to let your ear canals air out and reduce moisture buildup.
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > How to Protect Your Ears from Headphone Damage > Practice Proper Hygiene and Maintenance
passages.speaker: Allow your ears to breathe

passages.text: If you use headphones daily, consider scheduling annual hearing tests to monitor your ear health. Early detection of mild hearing changes can help prevent permanent damage and enable timely treatment or intervention. Hearing professionals can offer personalized advice on safe listening and device options suited to your needs. Proactive hearing care pays lifelong dividends.
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > How to Protect Your Ears from Headphone Damage > Regular Hearing Check-Ups

passages.text: Early intervention is crucial when addressing ear health concerns related to headphone use.
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > What To Do If You Experience Symptoms

passages.text: Persistent tinnitus or hearing difficulties? Schedule an appointment with an ear, nose, and throat (ENT) specialist if symptoms persist beyond a few days or worsen.
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > What To Do If You Experience Symptoms

passages.text: Signs of infection or inflammation (pain, itching, discharge)? Seek medical evaluation promptly. Treatment might include antibiotics, antifungal medications, or topical therapies as appropriate.
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > What To Do If You Experience Symptoms

passages.text: Hearing aids or therapies: In confirmed cases of noise-induced hearing loss, assistive devices or hearing therapy can improve quality of life.
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > What To Do If You Experience Symptoms
passages.speaker: Hearing aids or therapies

passages.text: Severe pain or sudden hearing loss? These symptoms require urgent medical attention. Don’t delay seeking care if you experience sudden changes.
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > What To Do If You Experience Symptoms

passages.text: Yes—listening to loud sounds for long durations can damage the delicate hair cells in your inner ear, leading to noise-induced hearing loss that is irreversible. Adopting safe listening habits is the most effective prevention.
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > Common Questions About Headphones and Ear Health > Can chronic headphone use really cause permanent hearing loss?

passages.text: Generally, yes! By blocking out background noise, noise-canceling headphones allow you to listen at lower volumes without sacrificing sound quality, helping reduce the risk of hearing damage.
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > Common Questions About Headphones and Ear Health > Are noise-canceling headphones safer for my ear health?

passages.text: If headphones are part of your daily life, an annual hearing evaluation is a smart preventive measure—especially if you notice any early symptoms of hearing changes.
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > Common Questions About Headphones and Ear Health > How often should I get my hearing checked?

passages.text: Use a dry or lightly damp cloth to wipe them regularly, avoiding soaking or submerging. Clean them several times a week, particularly after sweating or sharing devices.
passages.heading_path: Chronic Headphone Use and Its Impact on Ear Health: Risks and Prevention > Common Questions About Headphones and Ear Health > What’s the best way to clean my headphones and earbuds?

passages.text: Yes, over-ear headphones tend to allow better ventilation compared to in-ear earbuds, which can trap moisture. However, regardless of type, practicing good hygiene is essential to minimize infection risk.

passages.text: Headphones are an incredible tool for modern life, enabling seamless communication and entertainment. However, their impact on ear health is real—from noise-induced hearing loss and infections to discomfort and irritation. The best way to enjoy your favorite sounds is to stay mindful: keep volumes at safe levels, limit total listening time, maintain headphone hygiene, and schedule regular hearing check-ups.

However, while everybody knows that explosive noise like construction equipment and jet engines can damage your ears, fewer people are aware of another, more common culprit. I'm speaking about music.

passages.text: These days, I expect most people own a smartphone that they use to listen to music. passages.heading_path: Earbuds vs. Headphones: Ear Doctors Reveal Which Is Safer

passages.text: Those listening devices fit into some pretty dank nooks and crannies. For anyone concerned with both sound quality and ear health, experts share which is better for which type of listener.
passages.heading_path: Earbuds vs. Headphones: Ear Doctors Reveal Which Is Safer

passages.text: Getty images (2)
passages.heading_path: Earbuds vs. Headphones: Ear Doctors Reveal Which Is Safer

passages.text: Whether it’s for commuting, exercising, or a little background enjoyment while you work, headphones and earbuds have become nearly as essential to our daily routines as the smartphones they often connect to. But if you’ve ever wondered if one is better than the other when it comes to your health, experts weigh in with a resounding yes. Some sources suggest that these devices can harbor bacteria levels up to 2,700 times greater than those found on an average cutting board and 330 times more than on a kitchen countertop. Maybe it’s no wonder some doctors are saying ear infections have increased in the past couple years.
passages.heading_path: Earbuds vs. Headphones: Ear Doctors Reveal Which Is Safer

passages.text: Ahead, we share insights from audiologists and ear, nose, and throat (ENT) MDs to uncover critical health differences between earbuds and headphones—and whether there is a cleaner, safer choice for your unique ears.
passages.heading_path: Earbuds vs. Headphones: Ear Doctors Reveal Which Is Safer

passages.text: How To Clean AirPods (and How Often You Should Clean Them)
passages.heading_path: Earbuds vs. Headphones: Ear Doctors Reveal Which Is Safer

passages.text: The level of sanitation between earbuds and headphones largely depends on their design and how they are used. Earbuds, which are inserted directly into the ear canal, create an enclosed environment that can foster bacterial growth and facilitate the transfer of microbes. Katie Dease, AuD, an audiologist with the Mayo Clinic , notes that earbuds contaminated with bacteria can introduce these organisms into the ear, potentially leading to infections like swimmer’s ear.
passages.heading_path: Earbuds vs. Headphones: Ear Doctors Reveal Which Is Safer > Earbuds vs. headphones: Which is more sanitary?

passages.text: Headphones, on the other hand, rest on the outer ear and do not penetrate as deeply, reducing direct contact with the sensitive inner ear areas. However, this does not automatically make headphones a more sanitary option. Both devices collect sweat, skin cells, and sebum. The key to maintaining hygiene with either device is regular cleaning with appropriate solutions—alcohol wipes are a good option—and keeping them dry and stored properly when not in use.
passages.heading_path: Earbuds vs. Headphones: Ear Doctors Reveal Which Is Safer > Earbuds vs. headphones: Which is more sanitary?

passages.text: Also, you should never share your earbuds with anyone . “You are introducing new and more numerous amounts of bacteria into your ear,” says Abbas Anwar, MD, board-certified otolaryngologist at Pacific Neuroscience Institute. “Also,” Dr. Anwar adds, “you probably don’t know if your friend has kept their earbuds clean. They can pick up all sorts of bacteria from different surfaces such as tables and purses, and these new ‘foreign’ bacteria can lead to infections in your ear.”
passages.heading_path: Earbuds vs. Headphones: Ear Doctors Reveal Which Is Safer > Earbuds vs. headphones: Which is more sanitary?

passages.text: Regarding potential damage to our ears, both devices carry risks if not used properly. The most significant concern is noise-induced hearing loss , which can occur from listening to loud volumes for prolonged periods. This danger is due to the damage to the tiny hairs in the inner ear, which are crucial for hearing. “They don’t regenerate. So you want to hang on to every little hair cell in the inner ear you can,” explains Colin Driscoll, MD, board-certified otolaryngologist, subspecialty certification in neurotology, and current chair of the department of otolaryngology at the Mayo Clinic .
passages.heading_path: Earbuds vs. Headphones: Ear Doctors Reveal Which Is Safer > Earbuds vs. headphones: Which is more damaging to your hearing?

passages.text: Earbuds are particularly concerning because they deliver sound directly into the ear canal, intensifying the sound pressure. In contrast, headphones spread the sound more externally, potentially reducing the direct pressure on the eardrum. However, both devices should be used responsibly—this means keeping the volume at an appropriate level and taking regular breaks to give your ears time to recover.
passages.heading_path: Earbuds vs. Headphones: Ear Doctors Reveal Which Is Safer > Earbuds vs. headphones: Which is more damaging to your hearing?

passages.text: Safe listening includes factoring in decibels and time. The higher the decibels, the less time you can listen safely at that level. “Listening at 80% volume for a maximum of 90 minutes at a time is the general rule of thumb,” advises Sharon Sandridge, PhD, audiologist and emeritus staff at the Cleveland Clinic . “It really is an inverse relationship between how long and how loud. If you are listening for over 90 minutes, the volume should be reduced so that the longer you listen, the lower the volume.” She also notes that if someone standing an arm’s length away can hear the music from your headphones or earbuds, or if you have to raise your voice to speak while listening, the volume is too loud.
passages.heading_path: Earbuds vs. Headphones: Ear Doctors Reveal Which Is Safer > Earbuds vs. headphones: Which is more damaging to your hearing?

passages.text: Another expert suggestion is to follow what some experts call the “60/60” rule: Use earbuds for no more than 60 minutes at a time and keep the volume under 60% of the maximum. After that, take at least a 60-minute break before using them again.
passages.heading_path: Earbuds vs. Headphones: Ear Doctors Reveal Which Is Safer > Earbuds vs. headphones: Which is more damaging to your hearing?

passages.text: Choosing the right audio equipment for workouts is crucial for those leading active lifestyles. Here, earbuds often have the upper hand: Many are specifically designed for exercise, offering features like sweat resistance and a secure fit that can handle vigorous movement without falling out.
passages.heading_path: Earbuds vs. Headphones: Ear Doctors Reveal Which Is Safer > Earbuds vs. headphones: Which is better for working out?

passages.text: While headphones sometimes offer better sound quality and battery life, they can be bulky and less resistant to heavy sweat. They might also not stay securely in place during high-impact activities like running or jumping.
passages.heading_path: Earbuds vs. Headphones: Ear Doctors Reveal Which Is Safer > Earbuds vs. headphones: Which is better for working out?

passages.text: Dr. Sandridge points out an important safety concern regarding isolating earbuds: These devices come with rubber tips that seal off the ear canal, offering excellent sound isolation. However, this isolation can become a hazard for runners or cyclists who must remain aware of their surroundings.
passages.heading_path: Earbuds vs. Headphones: Ear Doctors Reveal Which Is Safer > Earbuds vs. headphones: Which is better for working out?
passages.speaker: Dr. Sandridge points out an important safety concern regarding isolating earbuds

passages.text: Both earbuds and headphones can contribute to earwax build-up, but earbuds are particularly problematic because they are inserted into the ear canal. Brian Taylor, AuD , an audiologist and senior director of audiology at Signia, explains: “Individuals that regularly use earbuds tend to have increased issues with occlusive wax build-up because of frequent earbud insertion, increasing the chances of pushing wax deeper into the canal.”
passages.heading_path: Earbuds vs. Headphones: Ear Doctors Reveal Which Is Safer > Earbuds vs. headphones: Which causes earwax build-up?

passages.text: For those experiencing wax occlusion due to earbuds, Dr. Taylor recommends switching to circum-aural headphones. These headphones envelop the ears rather than entering the ear canal, which minimizes pressure on the ear canal and decreases the risk of wax impaction.
passages.heading_path: Earbuds vs. Headphones: Ear Doctors Reveal Which Is Safer > Earbuds vs. headphones: Which causes earwax build-up?

citations.sentence_text: The evidence indicates that over-ear headphones are generally safer than earbuds for long-term ear health, particularly regarding infection risk and earwax impaction.
citations.audit_note: Passage supports reduction in wax impaction risk but does not address infection risk.

citations.sentence_text: Headphones do not go into the ear canal, reducing the risk of ear infections and wax impaction.
citations.audit_note: Passage supports reduced wax impaction risk but not infection risk.

citations.sentence_text: Dr. Taylor, cited in The Healthy, recommends circum-aural headphones to minimize pressure on the ear canal and decrease wax impaction risk.
citations.audit_note: Passage supports Dr. Taylor's recommendation but does not cite The Healthy.

passages.text: While noise-canceling earbuds and headphones are great for minimizing background noise and improving focus and relaxation, wearing them for too long at high volumes can strain your ears and may cause long-term hearing damage. Additionally, wearing these devices for prolonged periods can trap moisture in the ears, creating an ideal environment for bacteria to grow.
passages.heading_path: Earbuds vs. Headphones: Ear Doctors Reveal Which Is Safer > Is it safe to wear noise-canceling earbuds or headphones all day?

passages.text: Taking regular breaks, limiting high-volume listening, and maintaining good hygiene with noise-canceling devices is important. This not only protects your ear’s health, but can also prolong the period of time your headphones or earbuds will stay functional.

passages.text: It’s estimated that 1 in 8 young people between the ages of 6 and 19 have hearing loss due to music blaring through earbuds or headphones. The numbers appear ready to worsen, too, as most children spend a few hours a day wearing audio devices.
passages.heading_path: Sound the Alarm: How Headphones Can Harm Your Hearing

passages.text: So, how can young ears be protected while rocking out? Audiologist Valerie Pavlovich Ruff, AuD , has some ideas.
passages.heading_path: Sound the Alarm: How Headphones Can Harm Your Hearing

passages.text: Video content: This video is available to watch online.

passages.heading_path: Sound the Alarm: How Headphones Can Harm Your Hearing > Why loud noise damages hearing

passages.text: The sounds of life come alive for you through the cochlea, a very sensitive organ in your inner ear . This spiral-shaped cavity contains two fluid-filled chambers lined with tiny hair cells that are topped with stereocilia, small hair-like structures that stimulate the hair cell.
passages.heading_path: Sound the Alarm: How Headphones Can Harm Your Hearing > Why loud noise damages hearing

passages.text: Nerve endings in these hair cells convert sound waves into electronic signals that your brain “hears.” (This process is known as mechanoelectrical transduction.)
passages.heading_path: Sound the Alarm: How Headphones Can Harm Your Hearing > Why loud noise damages hearing

passages.text: If you pound your ears with loud sounds, it takes a toll on this delicate mechanism. “These sensory cells can actually be injured by exposure to loud music or loud noise for too long,” says Dr. Ruff.
passages.heading_path: Sound the Alarm: How Headphones Can Harm Your Hearing > Why loud noise damages hearing

passages.text: Repeated exposure to loud noise can cause irreparable damage over time. Overloaded ears age 50% faster than ears not pounded by sound. So, by the time you’re entering your 50s, you may have the hearing of someone in their 80s.
passages.heading_path: Sound the Alarm: How Headphones Can Harm Your Hearing > Why loud noise damages hearing

passages.text: “You cannot just fix this cumulative damage,” she explains. “Those sensory cells will no longer allow you to hear at certain frequencies. They’re just gone.”
passages.heading_path: Sound the Alarm: How Headphones Can Harm Your Hearing > Why loud noise damages hearing

passages.text: Signs of noise-induced hearing loss from earbuds, headphones or other loud sources include:
passages.heading_path: Sound the Alarm: How Headphones Can Harm Your Hearing > Why loud noise damages hearing

passages.text: Ringing in your ears ( tinnitus ).
passages.heading_path: Sound the Alarm: How Headphones Can Harm Your Hearing > Why loud noise damages hearing

passages.text: An inability to hear higher-pitched sounds (like birds singing).
passages.heading_path: Sound the Alarm: How Headphones Can Harm Your Hearing > Why loud noise damages hearing

passages.text: Muffled sounds and difficulty following conversations.
passages.heading_path: Sound the Alarm: How Headphones Can Harm Your Hearing > Why loud noise damages hearing

passages.text: Sound intensity is measured in decibels (dB), a logarithmic scale showing exponential increases. In this system, a noise that increases from 80 dB to 90 dB is 10 times more intense for your ears and will seem about twice as loud.
passages.heading_path: Sound the Alarm: How Headphones Can Harm Your Hearing > Why loud noise damages hearing > How loud is too loud?

passages.text: When dialed up to max volume, smartphones and tablets can blare at up to 110 dB over headphones or earbuds — a sound intensity that can cause damage to ears in as little as five minutes.
passages.heading_path: Sound the Alarm: How Headphones Can Harm Your Hearing > Why loud noise damages hearing > How loud is too loud?

passages.text: “If you walk by someone and can hear what’s on their headphones, the sound is too loud,” says Dr. Ruff.
passages.heading_path: Sound the Alarm: How Headphones Can Harm Your Hearing > Why loud noise damages hearing > How loud is too loud?

passages.text: So, what’s safe for your ears? The World Health Organization (WHO) considers 80 dB the line for a safe listening environment over an eight-hour workday. (In the U.S., the Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) sets the standard at 85 dB.)
passages.heading_path: Sound the Alarm: How Headphones Can Harm Your Hearing > Why loud noise damages hearing > How loud is too loud?

passages.text: To put that in perspective, 80 dB is the noise level you’d expect in a crowded restaurant, while 85 dB equates to what you’d hear standing along a busy roadway.
passages.heading_path: Sound the Alarm: How Headphones Can Harm Your Hearing > Why loud noise damages hearing > How loud is too loud?

passages.text: As the dBs go up, the amount of time you can be safely exposed to the louder sound quickly drops, notes Dr. Ruff. An increase of 3 dB cuts your “safe” listening time in half ­— meaning your ears can only handle minutes when noise levels climb above 100 dB.
passages.heading_path: Sound the Alarm: How Headphones Can Harm Your Hearing > Why loud noise damages hearing > How loud is too loud?

passages.text: Now, the good news: Noise-induced hearing loss from headphones or earbuds is avoidable. “It is in our power to prevent this damage to our ears,” shares Dr. Ruff. “It just takes a little awareness and effort.”
passages.heading_path: Sound the Alarm: How Headphones Can Harm Your Hearing > Tips to safely use headphones

passages.text: Here are four ways to keep your hearing intact while using earbuds or headphones.
passages.heading_path: Sound the Alarm: How Headphones Can Harm Your Hearing > Tips to safely use headphones

passages.text: Every listening device includes volume controls. How you use them may help determine how well you hear in the future, as volume level and length of listening are the key factors in sound-induced hearing loss.
passages.heading_path: Sound the Alarm: How Headphones Can Harm Your Hearing > Tips to safely use headphones > 1. Turn the sound down

passages.text: “If you’re listening at 50% to 60% of your max volume, you can probably safely listen to music most of the day,” says Dr. Ruff.
passages.heading_path: Sound the Alarm: How Headphones Can Harm Your Hearing > Tips to safely use headphones > 1. Turn the sound down

passages.text: But if you turn the sound up, you’ll need to give your ears a break. A good rule of thumb is to limit your listening time to about 90 minutes if you have the volume set at about 80% of the maximum.
passages.heading_path: Sound the Alarm: How Headphones Can Harm Your Hearing > Tips to safely use headphones > 1. Turn the sound down

passages.text: Earbuds that don’t fit in your ears very well tend to let in a lot of surrounding noise, which makes it tough to listen to your music or podcast. The same can be said for headphones that sit loosely over your ears.
passages.heading_path: Sound the Alarm: How Headphones Can Harm Your Hearing > Tips to safely use headphones > 2. Avoid poor-fitting listening devices

passages.text: What do you do in either case? Odds are, you turn up the volume to compensate. “That’s a formula to injury for the inner ear,” states Dr. Ruff.
passages.heading_path: Sound the Alarm: How Headphones Can Harm Your Hearing > Tips to safely use headphones > 2. Avoid poor-fitting listening devices

passages.text: Try to find noise-canceling earbuds that form a tight seal inside the ear canal to block out the surrounding sounds and allow you to keep the volume lower. Headphones should fit snugly over your ears.
passages.heading_path: Sound the Alarm: How Headphones Can Harm Your Hearing > Tips to safely use headphones > 2. Avoid poor-fitting listening devices

passages.text: A word of caution, though: Using “noise-canceling” devices means you might not hear important warning sounds like car horns if you’re out and about. These types of devices are best used when you’re in a secure setting.
passages.heading_path: Sound the Alarm: How Headphones Can Harm Your Hearing > Tips to safely use headphones > 2. Avoid poor-fitting listening devices

passages.text: Higher-quality headphones or earbuds typically provide a better sound. “That makes it less likely that you’ll rely on volume to enhance the fidelity,” says Dr. Ruff.
passages.heading_path: Sound the Alarm: How Headphones Can Harm Your Hearing > Tips to safely use headphones > 3. Opt for quality devices

passages.text: Both earbuds and headphones come in volume-limiting styles. These listening devices keep sound levels below the danger level, so they’re a great choice for anyone who tends to crank up the volume.
passages.heading_path: Sound the Alarm: How Headphones Can Harm Your Hearing > Tips to safely use headphones > 4. Use sound-limiting technology

passages.text: Various apps installed on listening devices can also keep noise levels at a safe level by limiting just how loud the volume can go.
passages.heading_path: Sound the Alarm: How Headphones Can Harm Your Hearing > Tips to safely use headphones > 4. Use sound-limiting technology

passages.text: “Any type of device that has a sound limiter is preferred,” notes Dr. Ruff.
passages.heading_path: Sound the Alarm: How Headphones Can Harm Your Hearing > Tips to safely use headphones > 4. Use sound-limiting technology

passages.text: It’s safe to say that headphone-wearing kids (or anyone, for that matter) don’t always think about their future hearing when they crank up the volume for their favorite song. It’s an instant gratification moment.
passages.heading_path: Sound the Alarm: How Headphones Can Harm Your Hearing > Build healthy listening habits

passages.text: But those damaging habits will take a toll. That’s why it’s important to start building good listening habits early in life. Programs have begun to teach children how to limit noise-induced hearing loss.
passages.heading_path: Sound the Alarm: How Headphones Can Harm Your Hearing > Build healthy listening habits

passages.text: “You get one set of ears in life and they can’t be replaced,” emphasizes Dr. Ruff. “If you’re using headphones or earbuds, it’s important to train yourself to listen to music at a softer level.”
passages.heading_path: Sound the Alarm: How Headphones Can Harm Your Hearing > Build healthy listening habits

passages.text: By doing so, you increase your odds of enjoying those sounds for years to come.
